e.etymology: A pet form of names beginning with Lu-, such as Lucretia, Lucinda and Louisa.
From the surname of Martin Van Buren, the eighth president. Van Buren means from Buren, a town in the Dutch province of Gelderland.
A surname from the English place name Boscombe. In the South it was often given in honor of Henry Bascom, a 19th-century Methodist bishop and preacher.
The Southern double name Willie Mae written as one word. Willie is a pet form of Wilhelmina or a feminine use of William, and Mae a form of May or Mary.
A Japanese girls' name ending in ko, child. The first part depends on the kanji; the commonest is fumi, writing or literature, and another spelling means abundant beauty.
The Icelandic and Swedish form of Old Norse Hildr, battle, the name of a valkyrie. Swedish immigrants brought it to America around 1900.
A contracted form of Caledonia, the Roman name for northern Britain and a poetic name for Scotland. Louis Jordan's 1945 hit song Caldonia kept the name in American ears.
The English word used as a virtue-style name, chiefly for boys in the 18th- and 19th-century American South.
An English surname from Audley in Staffordshire, a place name meaning the woodland clearing of a woman named Aldgyth.
The battlefield nickname of Confederate general Thomas J. Jackson, said to have stood like a stone wall at First Bull Run in 1861. Southern families gave it to sons for decades after the Civil War.

assoc.t: Stonewall uprising of 1969, a turning point for gay rights

e.note: Honors a Confederate general; the word is now just as tied to the 1969 Stonewall uprising.

e.etymology: A Japanese girls' name ending in ko, child. The first part depends on the kanji; spring is the most familiar reading, and clear weather is another.
A Japanese boys' name from the verb minoru, to ripen or bear fruit, usually written with a single kanji.
A spelling of Bessie or Bess, old English pet forms of Elizabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath.

e.note: Sounds like Arby's, the roast beef sandwich chain.

e.etymology: A spelling of Barney, the pet form of Barnabas, the apostle's name explained in Acts as son of encouragement, and of Bernard, Germanic for brave as a bear.
e.note: Sounds the same as Barney, so the purple dinosaur and Barney Fife come along with it.

e.etymology: A pet form of Della or Delia, or of longer names such as Adeline and Cordelia.
A spelling of Hardy, a surname from Old French and Middle English hardi, bold or brave. Hardie is the usual Scottish spelling of the surname.
A spelling of Herbert, from Germanic hari, army, and beraht, bright, that leans toward the sound of Hubert.
A spelling of Lela that records the Southern habit of sounding a final -a as -er, also seen in Ellar and Dellar.
From the pen name of the French Enlightenment writer the Comte de Volney, who formed it from Voltaire and Ferney, the name of Voltaire's estate. His book The Ruins was widely read in early America.
A short form of Tatiana, the feminine of the Roman family name Tatius, whose meaning is unknown.
An old American given name, as in the abolitionist preacher Orange Scott. It may honor William of Orange, whose title came from the town of Orange in southern France.
e.note: Reads as the fruit and the color before it reads as a name.

e.etymology: A short form of Reuben, Hebrew for behold, a son, the name of Jacob's eldest son in Genesis.
namesakes: Rube Goldberg (cartoonist whose name means a comically overbuilt machine)

assoc.t: a rube, an unsophisticated country person
Rube Goldberg machine, an absurdly complex contraption

e.note: Rube is slang for a naive country person, a sense that came from this nickname.

e.etymology: A spelling of Mabel, a medieval short form of Amabel, from Latin amabilis, lovable.
